text: Port 21 is open. On its own, that's barely useful — dozens of FTP server implementations exist, spanning two decades of patch history, and whether that's a real finding depends entirely on which one, and which version. Enumeration is the step that turns a port number into an exact answer, and it's where a scanning phase actually earns its time.

Nmap's -sV flag sends a sequence of probes from its service-probes database and compares the responses against known signatures. That's how it tells Apache apart from nginx even though both answer as http, and pulls out an exact version string where it can. Here, vsftpd 2.3.4 isn't a neutral detail — it's a specific, publicly known-backdoored build, exactly the kind of exact-version hit worth cross-referencing further.

You can control how hard -sV works with --version-intensity, zero through nine: lower sends only the most common probes and finishes fast, nine tries everything in the database and finishes slow but thorough. -A is a convenience flag that bundles version detection with OS fingerprinting, default scripts, and traceroute into a single run, when you want the fuller picture in one pass.

Automated detection isn't infallible — banners get reconfigured to hide or spoof themselves. Connecting by hand with netcat, nc -nv target 21, reads whatever greeting the service sends unprompted with no interpretation layer in between. And the Nmap Scripting Engine, -sC or a targeted --script, pulls detail version detection alone won't show: HTTP titles, certificate info, SMB OS discovery.

Some services need a dedicated tool. enum4linux -a against a Windows host can pull SMB share names, domain info, and sometimes user lists, often without authentication if the target is misconfigured. snmpwalk against a default community string can leak an entire device's configuration. Neither is an Nmap flag, but it's the same discipline — keep enumerating past 'the port is open' until you actually know what's there.

You now have exact software and versions, not just port numbers — real leads worth checking against what's known to be vulnerable. The next lesson covers vulnerability scanning itself: what a tool like Nessus or OpenVAS adds on top of this, the real difference authenticated scanning makes, and exactly why a clean scanner report is never the same thing as a finished pentest.
